The result was a wave of privatization across more than 90 countries. Today, more than 850 airports worldwide have some form of private investment. In Europe, 76% of all passenger traffic moves through privately owned airports. In Latin America, 78%. The United States is almost entirely the opposite. American airports are still owned by city and state governments. The only major commercial airport fully privatized under the federal program is Luis Muñoz Marín International in San Juan, Puerto Rico. JFK, LAX, O'Hare, Atlanta, all publicly owned. Okay, so you want to buy an airport,
find a piece of land, build a runway,
let the planes land, collect the fees.

It sounds like the closest thing the
modern world has to a toll booth.

One

uses it pays you.
evidence.excerpt_end: You are by definition the only option.

evidence.excerpt:
So, you sit back, watch the planes
arrive, and let the money come in.

That
is the dream, and it is not entirely
wrong.
evidence.excerpt_end:
For most of history, governments built
airports and owned them, public
infrastructure paid for by taxpayers.

evidence.excerpt:
But, starting in the 1980s, something
changed.

Governments realized they were
sitting on enormously valuable assets,
and private investors realized that a
monopoly with guaranteed traffic was
exactly the kind of thing you want to
own for the next 50 years.

The result
was a wave of privatization across more
than 90 countries.

Today, more than 850
airports worldwide have some form of
private investment.
evidence.excerpt_end:
Governments sell
airports in one of three ways.

evidence.excerpt:
An
outright sale, a long-term concession
where the buyer takes control for 40 to
99 years and then hands it back, or a
public stock offering.

The concession model has become the most
popular because it lets governments
raise money without fully surrendering
the asset.
evidence.excerpt_end:
When investors value an airport,
they compare the purchase price against
EBITDA, the money the business earns
before paying interest, taxes, and
accounting adjustments.

evidence.excerpt:
A healthy
airport sells for between 15 and 23
times its annual EBITDA.

The Sydney deal was struck during a
pandemic when travel had collapsed.
evidence.excerpt_end:
Acquiring that land, clearing title,
compensating everyone displaced, and
ensuring it avoids protected zones costs
hundreds of millions before a single
foundation is poured.

over a billion dollars in most developed
countries.
